A Fresh Approach to Updatable Symmetric Encryption (https://eprint.iacr.org/2021/559.pdf)
【turn344818view0】 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: 1.4 years ago; Content type: application/pdf; Number of pages: 46; Source: open({"ref_id":"https://eprint.iacr.org/2021/559.pdf","lineno":null}); Total lines: 2394
L0@P0: A Fresh Approach to Updatable Symmetric
L1@P0: Encryption
L2@P0: Andr´es Fabrega1, Ueli Maurer2, and Marta Mularczyk2?
L3@P0: 1
L4@P0: andresfg@mit.edu, MIT
L5@P0: 2
L6@P0: {maurer,mumarta}@inf.ethz.ch, ETH Zurich
L7@P0: Abstract. Updatable encryption (UE) is symmetric encryption which
L8@P0: additionally supports key rotation. UE was introduced for scenarios where
L9@P0: a user stores encrypted data on a cloud and, in order to mitigate secret
L10@P0: key leakage, periodically sends a short update token, which the cloud
L11@P0: uses to re-encrypt stored data to a fresh key. A long line of research resulted in a wide variety of security properties UE schemes can provide,
L12@P0: including confidentiality, integrity protection, and hiding metadata. Unfortunately, given the complexity and nuances in the definitions, different properties are difficult to compare for non-experts, making it hard
L13@P0: to judge which scheme provides the best security-efficiency trade-off for
L14@P0: a given application.
L15@P0: In this work, we challenge the approach of defining UE as a primitive
L16@P0: with a set of properties. As an alternative, we propose to treat UE as
L17@P0: an interactive protocol, whose goal is to implement secure outsourced
L18@P0: storage, using limited and imperfect resources (such as a small, leakable memory). To facilitate this approach, we introduce a framework
L19@P0: that allows to easily formalize different security guarantees and available
L20@P0: resources, making security-efficiency trade-offs of UE protocols easy to
L21@P0: compare.
L22@P0: We believe that our approach opens the way for many constructions
L23@P0: of secure storage that are not compatible with the currently defined
L24@P0: syntax of UE. Indeed, we propose two new protocols: one for the setting
L25@P0: with adversaries who control randomness (an attack vector so far not
L26@P0: considered for UE), and one for the setting with adversaries that actively
L27@P0: tamper with memory. Both protocols provide stronger confidentiality
L28@P0: guarantees than all existing UE schemes.
L29@P0: 1 Introduction
L30@P0: 1.1 Updatable Encryption
L31@P0: Key rotation and updatable encryption. In today’s globalized world, the need
L32@P0: for (private) data to be constantly available on many devices and to many (authorized) users is evident. A natural way to achieve this is outsourcing storage,
L33@P0-1: ? Research supported by the Zurich Information Security and Privacy Center (ZISC).namely, uploading data to a commercial platform (often called a cloud). Unfortunately, this introduces new attack vectors, as the platform cannot be trusted
L34@P1: to always protect confidentiality and integrity of data. To prevent these new
L35@P1: attacks, data is encrypted and the secret key is distributed among authorized
L36@P1: devices. However, this is still not fully satisfactory, since, first, devices may get
L37@P1: compromised and reveal the key (e.g. if they are lost or catch a virus) and, second, a key should not be used too many times (e.g. due to cryptanalytic attacks).
L38@P1: Mitigating these attacks is the goal of key rotation, which mandates periodically
L39@P1: replacing the key under which (already stored) data is encrypted.
L40@P1: Efficiently implementing an outsourced storage service that supports key rotation is not an easy task. Let us first state the goal more precisely. For simplicity,
L41@P1: from now on we consider only two parties: the host, i.e. the platform where data
L42@P1: is uploaded, and the data owner, who represents all entities that can access
L43@P1: the data.3 They are both honest, but also careless — any piece of information
L44@P1: they see or store, such as a key or a received message, may potentially leak to
L45@P1: the adversary or be modified by her. The goal is to design a protocol for the
L46@P1: parties that constructs a storage service for the owner, which protects confidentiality and integrity of as many stored messages as possible, given which pieces
L47@P1: of information leaked or were corrupted.
L48@P1: The obvious approaches to achieve this are either insecure or inefficient. For
L49@P1: example, if one uses standard symmetric encryption, it is not clear how to implement key rotation: sending the old and the new key to the host achieves suboptimal security, because information sent to the host is sufficient to decrypt
L50@P1: all messages. Alternatively, the owner could download all data and re-encrypt it
L51@P1: himself, but this is clearly not efficient.
L52@P1: Enabling more efficient protocols is the goal of updatable encryption (UE)
L53@P1: introduced by Boneh et al.[BLMR13]. In essence, UE has the functionality of
L54@P1: symmetric encryption, but offers two additional algorithms for key rotation: nxt
L55@P1: (meant for the owner), given the old and the fresh key, generates a short update
L56@P1: token, and upd (for the host), given a token and a ciphertext, updates it to the
L57@P1: new key. Importantly, the token does not reveal any information about the keys.
L58@P1: Defining secure UE. UE has received considerable attention in the cryptographic
L59@P1: community [BLMR13, EPRS17, LT18, KLR19, BDGJ20, Jia20, BEKS20, CLT20].
L60@P1: It comes in surprisingly many flavors and with many different security properties. First, there are multiple versions of syntax. For example, ciphertextindependent UE, where nxt generates a single token for all ciphertexts and
L61@P1: ciphertext-dependent UE, where nxt generates one token per ciphertext and gets
L62@P1: as input the ciphertext’s short header (sent by the host). Independently, one can
L63@P1: consider deterministic or randomized upd algorithm. Regarding security properties, there are notions analogous to IND-CPA, IND-RCCA and IND-CCA. The
L64@P1: properties related to integrity include analogues of INT-PTXT and INT-CTXT.
L65@P1: 3 Considering a single owner, we implicitly assume that there is an external mechanism
L66@P1: which synchronizes all devices. Achieving this is outside the scope of this work.
L67@P1-2: 2There are also properties formalizing secrecy of metadata, such as how many
L68@P2: times a ciphertext has been updated.
L69@P2: Different syntaxes and security properties offer different trade-offs between
L70@P2: security and efficiency, which are not always obvious to compare. This makes the
L71@P2: task of choosing the right scheme for given application difficult. For instance,
L72@P2: randomized upd is less efficient in terms of randomness and one cannot meaningfully define IND-CCA for it. However, it allows to achieve an additional property
L73@P2: that an updated ciphertext looks like a fresh encryption even given the previous
L74@P2: ciphertext and update token. As another example, notions that consider active
L75@P2: attackers are defined slightly differently in different papers. Namely, sometimes
L76@P2: the adversary can inject arbitrary ciphertexts only to the decryption algorithm
L77@P2: (e.g. IND-CCA in [BDGJ20]), and sometimes to both decryption and upd (e.g.
L78@P2: IND-RCCA in [KLR19]). Intuitively, the first version appears too weak, since it
L79@P2: offers no guarantees if an active attacker modifies the host’s storage and then
L80@P2: the host applies upd. On the other hand, it is much more common in the UE
L81@P2: literature and the difference is sometimes not made explicit.
L82@P2: 1.2 Contributions
L83@P2: We claim that viewing UE as a primitive with a fixed syntax and a set of security
L84@P2: properties is perhaps too restrictive. Instead, we propose a different approach,
L85@P2: where we directly formalize the goal of UE. That is, UE is not a scheme but
L86@P2: an interactive protocol between the owner and the host, the goal of which is
L87@P2: to implement a secure storage service in the setting where different pieces of
L88@P2: information may leak to the adversary or be modified by her.
L89@P2: Our modeling framework offers more flexibility than the standard approach
L90@P2: and makes it easy to express different confidentiality and integrity guarantees.
L91@P2: Moreover, it precisely formalizes resources required by protocols (such as channels and storage), making the security-efficiency trade-offs achieved by different
L92@P2: constructions easy to see. Our framework generalizes all existing definitions, as
L93@P2: well as enables finding new trade-offs, which would require UE with yet different
L94@P2: syntax.
L95@P2: We then give three instantiations of our framework, focusing on ciphertextindependent UE. The first explains the known notion of IND-CPA security. In
L96@P2: the second instantiation, we consider the setting where the adversary can control
L97@P2: randomness, an attack vector so far not considered for UE. Not being constrained
L98@P2: by any fixed syntax, we design a scheme with better bad-randomness resistance
L99@P2: than what is possible with any existing syntax. Our construction is very simple
L100@P2: and ready to implement in practice. Finally, the third instantiation considers
L101@P2: active attackers who can modify the host’s storage. While this attack vector is
L102@P2: more realistic than, e.g., injecting messages on the channel (since the storage
L103@P2: is long-lived), most existing security notions are not suitable, as they offer no
L104@P2: guarantees if the host updates injected ciphertexts. Our construction protects
L105@P2: confidentiality of data against active attackers. It builds on a suitable IND-RCCA
L106@P2: secure UE scheme [LT18].
L107@P2-3: 3Framework for defining UE. In particular, we define security of UE protocols
L108@P3: using the simulation-based paradigm, in a composable framework. This means
L109@P3: that the real-world execution of a UE protocol should be indistinguishable from
L110@P3: the ideal-world execution, where a trusted storage service keeps the owner’s
L111@P3: messages secret and all leaked information is simulated without them.
L112@P3: More precisely, the real world consists of a number of limited and imperfect
L113@P3: resources: memories, channels and randomness sources (then the protocol must
L114@P3: be deterministic and stateless). Each resource has bounded capacity and can
L115@P3: only be used once, which formalizes efficiency. Moreover, the adversary may
L116@P3: corrupt each resource and obtain read and/or write access to the contents (i.e.,
L117@P3: the stored, sent or sampled value). Finally, to express assumptions about the
L118@P3: real world (e.g. authenticated channel), each resource is parameterized by two
L119@P3: predicates: can-leak and can-inject, which control the adversary’s read and write
L120@P3: access, respectively. The leakability and injectability guarantees of a resource
L121@P3: may change over time, for example, the first channel is leakable only once the
L122@P3: second channel leaks. This is expressed using events [JMM19]: each resource can
L123@P3: trigger events, such as leaked, and the global list of all events that happened so
L124@P3: far is the input to can-leak and can-inject predicates.
L125@P3: The ideal world, on the other hand, consists of the secure storage service and
L126@P3: a simulator. The ideal storage formalizes security of a UE protocol. It allows the
L127@P3: owner to store, retrieve and delete messages, as well as to update all ciphertexts
L128@P3: at once. Then, it gives to the simulator read and/or write access to only a subset
L129@P3: of stored messages. Whether the access to a message is granted is determined by
L130@P3: the can-leak and can-inject predicates, parameters of the storage. As in the real
L131@P3: world, they can depend on the list of all events (such as the owner updating).
L132@P3: We highlight some relevant points of our model:
L133@P3: – Flexible assumptions and guarantees. Different assumptions and guarantees
L134@P3: can be expressed by adjusting can-leak and can-inject predicates in the real
L135@P3: and the ideal world, respectively.
L136@P3: – Clear semantics. The semantics of our statements are simple — one can
L137@P3: think of the protocol as of the idealized trusted storage — making it easy
L138@P3: to judge if a statement is suited for a given application. In contrast, for
L139@P3: game-based definitions, judging if a given combination of security properties
L140@P3: is exactly what is needed tends to be hard.
L141@P3: – Flexible syntax and comparable efficiency. The protocol can use its resources
L142@P3: in an arbitrary way, and the assumed resources make it easy to compare
L143@P3: efficiency. For instance, a protocol using ciphertext-dependent UE simply
L144@P3: requires more channels, on which the host can send all ciphertext headers.
L145@P3: In a different protocol, the host could collect information from all stored
L146@P3: ciphertexts into a single shorter header. Such protocol would have efficiency
L147@P3: between ciphertext-dependent and ciphertext-independent UE. (Its security
L148@P3: guarantees would probably also be in between, since leaking the token would
L149@P3: not affect messages stored after it is created.) This and many other examples
L150@P3: show that hard-coding the syntax is unnecessarily restrictive.
L151@P3-4: 4– Stronger statements. The type of statements we make is that a protocol improves arbitrary guarantees of real-world resources. For example, a protocol
L152@P4: using IND-CCA secure UE should improve confidentiality, while preserving
L153@P4: integrity protection. This is stronger than a standard statement formalizing
L154@P4: IND-CCA, where the real-world resources are always injectable.
L155@P4: – Easy to extend. While we focus on memory, channels and randomness, one
L156@P4: can easily model different assumptions, such as a common reference string.
L157@P4: This may enable more efficient solutions than standard UE.
L158@P4: Randomness corruption. As bad randomness generators are a very realistic attack vector (a well-known example is the backdoored DualEC PRNG [SS06,
L159@P4: SF07]), it comes as a surprise that they have never been considered in the context of UE. In fact, existing schemes achieve very different guarantees in the
L160@P4: presence of attackers who can corrupt randomness. For example, consider leaking randomness used to encrypt a message. With the RISE scheme [LT18] (where
L161@P4: encryption is essentially ElGamal) this allows to decrypt the message, while the
L162@P4: BLMR [BLMR13] and SHINE [BDGJ20] schemes remain secure. Second, consider leaking randomness used by nxt to generate a token. The way SHINE is
L163@P4: defined, nxt first chooses the new key at random, and then computes the token
L164@P4: using both keys. This means that leaked randomness contains the new key and
L165@P4: can be used to decrypt all ciphertexts. An equivalent way to define SHINE is to
L166@P4: generate the token at random and compute the new key. Intuitively, this is more
L167@P4: secure, since the token cannot be used to decrypt.
L168@P4: In this work, we propose a construction that improves upon all existing
L169@P4: schemes. Our protocol is for the setting where randomness may be chosen by
L170@P4: the adversary. Roughly, the first idea is to replace the randomized encryption
L171@P4: algorithm with one that is nonce-based and hence deterministic. This is done in
L172@P4: a generic way, using a PRF, as in [Rog04]. This is clearly better, since nonces do
L173@P4: not need to be secret. To choose the nonce, our protocol assumes that each stored
L174@P4: message has a unique identifier. This assumption seems reasonable in practice
